title: Towards Open Evolutionary Agents
description: A 29-experiment study of OpenEvolve, an open-source evolutionary coding agent, on the AlgoTune benchmark: open models like Qwen3-Coder and Gemma 3 27B rival closed models, diff-based evolution beats full rewrites for strong coders, and combining models into an ensemble underperforms the best single model.
tldr: OpenEvolve, an open-source evolutionary coding agent, was run through 29 experiments on the AlgoTune benchmark. Open models such as Gemma 3 27B and Qwen3-Coder 480B matched or beat closed models, diff-based evolution outperformed full rewrites once models were capable enough to use it, parallel evaluation was essential (serial evaluation was 47 to 50 percent worse and 14 times slower), and an ensemble of the two best models underperformed either model alone.
abstract: We performed a comprehensive analysis of 29 experiments using OpenEvolve, an open-source evolutionary coding agent, on the AlgoTune{{cite:press2025algotune}} benchmark suite. Both proprietary and open models achieved significant performance gains. Open models such as Google's Gemma 3 27B and Alibaba's Qwen3-Coder 480B demonstrated impressive optimization capabilities, rivalling and sometimes uniquely surpassing their closed-source counterparts. Gemini Flash 2.5 achieved the top speedup of 2.04x, with Gemma 3 27B and Qwen3-Coder reaching 1.63x and 1.41x respectively. AlgoTune is a benchmark for algorithmic optimization capability, spanning graph algorithms, linear algebra, and optimization problems. Unlike benchmarks that grade only correctness, AlgoTune specifically measures performance improvement: each task provides a baseline implementation, and systems are scored on how much faster they can make it while remaining correct.

blocks.alt: A 2x2 dashboard of four panels: temperature comparison across 0.2/0.4/0.8, performance over 100 vs 200 iterations, all ten models at their best configuration, and the collapse in performance from serial evaluation.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. Executive dashboard. Panel A compares temperatures 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8. Panel B shows continued gains from 100 to 200 iterations. Panel C compares all ten models tested at their best configuration. Panel D shows the performance collapse under serial evaluation.

blocks.text: Across the 29 experiments, six findings stood out:

items: More iterations help: 200 iterations reached a 2.04x AlgoTune score versus 1.64x for 100 iterations, a 24% improvement.
Specialization beats size: Qwen3-Coder (480B mixture-of-experts, coding-specialized) outperformed the larger general-purpose Qwen3-235B model.
Evolution strategy is model-dependent: strong coding models do best with diff-based evolution, while weaker models need full rewrites.
Temperature optimization matters: 0.4 was optimal for Gemini models (1.29x versus 1.17x at temperature 0.2).
Artifacts boost performance: including debugging artifacts{{fn:artifacts-def}} in the evaluation feedback improved results by 17%.
Parallelism is critical: serial evaluation catastrophically fails, losing about 50% of performance and running 14 times slower.

blocks.caption: Table 1. Top performers across the 29 experiments, ranked by AlgoTune score.

blocks.text: Across all 29 runs, 10 unique models were tested (the Gemini, Qwen, Meta, and Google-open families, plus ensembles) against 30 AlgoTune benchmark tasks. The best overall result was Gemini Flash 2.5 at 2.04x (200 iterations). The worst was 0.396x, from serial diff-based evaluation, a roughly 50% degradation versus its parallel counterpart. Temperature was tested at 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8, evolution strategy as diff-based or full rewrite, and evaluation as parallel (16 workers) versus serial.

OpenEvolve{{cite:sharma2025openevolve}} is an open-source evolutionary coding agent that began as an implementation of DeepMind's AlphaEvolve{{cite:novikov2025alphaevolve}} and has since grown well beyond it, adding reproducibility tooling, multi-language support, and more sophisticated evaluation pipelines. It improves a program through a repeated loop: the model proposes an edit, an evaluator scores the result against the task's objective, and the strongest candidates survive to seed the next generation.
The experiments ran in two phases: an initial phase covering baseline testing and parameter tuning, followed by a second phase adding extended-iteration runs and newer models.
Ten models were tested across four families:

items: Gemini family: Flash 2.5 (Google's efficient coding model) and Flash 2.5 Lite (a smaller variant used for baseline testing).
Qwen family: Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct (480B mixture-of-experts with 35B active parameters, coding-specialized), Qwen3-235B-A22B (a general-purpose model), and Qwen3-32B (a smaller variant).
Other models: Gemma 3 27B (Google's open model) and Llama 3.3 70B (Meta's latest model).
Ensembles: configurations combining multiple models on the same task.

blocks.text: The 29 experiments break down into five categories: baseline testing (7 experiments), temperature study (3), parameter tuning (8), model comparison (6), and extended iterations (4).

items: 30 AlgoTune{{cite:press2025algotune}} tasks were converted to OpenEvolve's format using a conversion script, algotune_to_openevolve.py.
Tasks span several algorithm categories: graphs, linear algebra, and optimization.
Scoring follows AlgoTune's own convention: the harmonic mean of per-task speedups.
Island-based MAP-Elites{{cite:mouret2015mapelites}}: four islands evolve in parallel with periodic migration between them.
Cascade evaluation: candidates pass through quick validation, then performance testing, then full evaluation, so weak candidates are discarded cheaply before the expensive full run.
Two evolution strategies: diff-based evolution, which proposes incremental code changes, and full rewrite, which regenerates the entire function.

blocks.text: AlgoTune scores tasks on a logarithmic performance scale, which is converted back to a speedup factor:

blocks.html:
# AlgoTune score calculation
speedup = (10 ** (performance * 3)) - 1  # Convert from log scale
algotune_score = harmonic_mean(all_speedups)  # Overall benchmark score

blocks.text: The harmonic mean emphasizes consistent performance across all tasks: a model must perform well on all 30 benchmarks to achieve a high overall score, since one weak task pulls the score down more than an arithmetic mean would.
All 29 experiments are ranked by AlgoTune score in the original report's performance-rankings chart{{fn:rankings-chart}}. The top performers and per-phase results below cover the same ground.
Gemini Flash 2.5 Lite baseline. With full rewrite, temperature 0.8, and a 4k token budget, Flash 2.5 Lite reached 1.10x speedup, establishing the baseline for later comparisons.

Evolution strategy discovery. Comparing diff-based against full rewrite on Flash Lite showed full rewrite winning clearly: 1.10x versus 0.79x for diff-based. Inspecting the failed diffs showed the model struggling to produce meaningful incremental edits:

blocks.html:
# Attempted diff that failed
- for i in range(n):
-     if not visited[i]:
-         dfs(i)
+ for i in range(n):
+     if not visited[i]:
+         # Incomplete optimization
+         dfs(i)  # No actual improvement

blocks.text: Running Gemini Flash 2.5 for 200 iterations instead of 100 reached 2.04x speedup, a 24% improvement. The count_connected_components task reached 95.78x, and the optimal Union-Find-free approach was already found by iteration 2. Progress accumulated steadily over the run:

items: Iteration 10: 1.15x
Iteration 50: 1.48x
Iteration 100: 1.64x
Iteration 200: 2.04x

blocks.text: Serial evaluation (one task at a time) was compared against parallel evaluation (16 workers) for both evolution strategies:

blocks.caption: Table 5. Serial versus parallel evaluation, both evolution strategies.

blocks.text: Three insights follow from this comparison:

items: Performance catastrophe: serial evaluation produces 47 to 50% worse results.
Time explosion: serial evaluation runs 14 times slower (13 hours versus 0.9 hours).

Why it fails: there is no cross-task learning during evolution, timeout issues compound across serial tasks, evolution gets stuck on difficult tasks, and the opportunity for parallel discovery across tasks is lost.

blocks.text: Parallel evaluation is not an optional optimization here. It is essential for OpenEvolve to function properly.

subsections.title: Example 1: Count Connected Components - Algorithm Discovery

blocks.text: All models started from the same depth-first-search baseline (1.0x):

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    n = problem["num_nodes"]
    edges = problem["edges"]
    
    # Build adjacency list
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    
    # DFS to count components
    visited = [False] * n
    count = 0
    
    def dfs(node):
        visited[node] = True
        for neighbor in adj[node]:
            if not visited[neighbor]:
                dfs(neighbor)
    
    for i in range(n):
        if not visited[i]:
            dfs(i)
            count += 1
    
    return {"number_connected_components": count}

blocks.text: Gemini Flash 2.5 (200 iterations), 95.78x speedup. It switched from DFS to BFS with a deque, added early-termination checks, and used defensive get() lookups:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    n = problem.get("num_nodes", 0)
    edges = problem.get("edges", [])
    
    if n == 0:
        return {"number_connected_components": 0}
    
    # Build adjacency list with deque for O(1) operations
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    
    # BFS with early termination and efficient tracking
    visited = [False] * n
    count = 0
    from collections import deque
    
    for start in range(n):
        if visited[start]:
            continue
            
        # BFS for this component
        queue = deque([start])
        visited[start] = True
        
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            for neighbor in adj[node]:
                if not visited[neighbor]:
                    visited[neighbor] = True
                    queue.append(neighbor)
        
        count += 1
    
    return {"number_connected_components": count}

blocks.text: Qwen3-Coder (100 iterations), about 25x speedup. It found a completely different algorithm, Union-Find with path compression:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    n = problem["num_nodes"]
    edges = problem["edges"]
    
    # Union-Find approach - completely different algorithm!
    parent = list(range(n))
    
    def find(x):
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])  # Path compression
        return parent[x]
    
    def union(x, y):
        px, py = find(x), find(y)
        if px != py:
            parent[px] = py
    
    # Process edges
    for u, v in edges:
        union(u, v)
    
    # Count unique roots
    return {"number_connected_components": len(set(find(i) for i in range(n)))}

blocks.text: Union-Find gives near-constant-time operations per edge (O(α(n))) and uses less memory than the adjacency-list BFS, but converged to a smaller speedup here since the two models explored different regions of the search space.

subsections.title: Example 2: PSD Cone Projection - Incremental Optimization

blocks.text: The original implementation (1.0x baseline) did an eigendecomposition, clipped negative eigenvalues, and reconstructed the matrix:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    import numpy as np
    
    A = np.array(problem["matrix"])
    # Eigenvalue decomposition
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)
    # Set negative eigenvalues to zero
    eigenvalues[eigenvalues < 0] = 0
    # Reconstruct matrix
    A_psd = eigenvectors @ np.diag(eigenvalues) @ eigenvectors.T
    return {"projected_matrix": A_psd.tolist()}

blocks.text: Gemini Flash 2.5's diff-based evolution reached the final 32.7x speedup incrementally. At iteration 23, it vectorized the eigenvalue clip (1.8x):

blocks.html:
- eigenvalues[eigenvalues < 0] = 0
- A_psd = eigenvectors @ np.diag(eigenvalues) @ eigenvectors.T
+ # Vectorized operation
+ eigenvalues = np.maximum(eigenvalues, 0)
+ A_psd = eigenvectors @ np.diag(eigenvalues) @ eigenvectors.T

blocks.text: At iteration 67, it eliminated an intermediate array by folding the diagonal multiply into elementwise broadcasting (15.2x):

blocks.html:
- A_psd = eigenvectors @ np.diag(eigenvalues) @ eigenvectors.T
+ # Eliminate intermediate array
+ A_psd = (eigenvectors * eigenvalues) @ eigenvectors.T

blocks.text: By iteration 95, the function had converged to a compact one-line vectorized form at 32.7x speedup:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    import numpy as np
    
    A = np.array(problem["matrix"])
    w, v = np.linalg.eigh(A)
    # One-line vectorized operation
    A_psd = (v * np.maximum(w, 0)) @ v.T
    return {"projected_matrix": A_psd.tolist()}

blocks.text: Starting from a plain SciPy DCT call:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    import numpy as np
    from scipy.fftpack import dct
    
    signal = np.array(problem["signal"])
    return {"dct": dct(signal, type=1).tolist()}

blocks.text: Gemini Flash 2.5 and Qwen3-Coder, evolving independently, converged on the same fix, forcing the input to float64 before calling dct:

blocks.html:
# Gemini Flash 2.5
signal = np.array(problem["signal"], dtype=np.float64)
result = dct(signal, type=1, norm=None, overwrite_x=False)

# Qwen3-Coder
signal = np.asarray(problem["signal"], dtype=np.float64)
return {"dct": dct(signal, type=1).tolist()}

blocks.text: Both reached the same 6.48x speedup. Two different models independently discovering the identical fix is evidence that the optimal solution here is a single, discoverable optimum rather than one of several roughly-equal options.
Starting point:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    import hashlib
    
    data = problem["data"].encode('utf-8')
    hash_object = hashlib.sha256(data)
    return {"hash": hash_object.hexdigest()}

blocks.text: The best evolution found by multiple models only removed a redundant intermediate variable and an explicit encoding argument:

blocks.html:
def solve(problem):
    import hashlib
    
    return {"hash": hashlib.sha256(problem["data"].encode()).hexdigest()}

blocks.text: This only reached 1.1x speedup. SHA256 is bound by the hardware's hash throughput rather than by the Python wrapper around it, so there is little headroom for an evolutionary coding agent to find, regardless of model.

blocks.alt: A heatmap of speedup factors with models on one axis and AlgoTune tasks on the other, darker red indicating a higher speedup.
blocks.caption: Figure 2. Speedup factor achieved by each model on each AlgoTune task. Darker red indicates a higher speedup.

blocks.text: Count connected components shows the widest spread across models, 95x for Flash 2.5 versus about 15x for Gemma 3. PSD projection is more consistent, with every model landing in the 32 to 42x range. Hardware-bound tasks such as SHA256 show minimal improvement regardless of which model evolves them.

Qwen3-Coder (480B total parameters, 35B active as a mixture-of-experts model) is technically larger than Qwen3-235B, yet it reached 1.41x versus 0.84x, a 68% improvement, despite using fewer parameters at inference time. Coding specialization outperformed raw parameter count here, evidence that training data and task focus matter more than model size for this kind of work.

sections.title: Ensemble Experiments: Why More Models Is Not Better

blocks.text: Combining the two best performers, Gemini Flash 2.5 (1.64x) and Qwen3-Coder (1.41x), into a single ensemble reached only 1.23x, worse than either model individually.

blocks.alt: A four-panel figure: individual versus ensemble performance, per-task performance profiles for all three configurations, evolution progress over iterations, and a model-agreement heatmap across tasks.
blocks.caption: Figure 3. Ensemble analysis. Panel A compares individual model performance against the ensemble, which underperforms both. Panel B compares performance profiles across all 30 tasks for Gemini, Qwen, and the ensemble. Panel C compares evolution progress, with the ensemble showing irregular oscillation against smooth single-model progress. Panel D is a model-agreement heatmap across all 30 tasks, showing where the two models' proposed edits conflict.

blocks.text: The ensemble underperformed the expected 1.5 to 1.7x range by 19%. Two conflicts explain most of the gap:

items: Count connected components: Gemini proposed BFS, Qwen proposed Union-Find, and alternating between them across iterations caused oscillation instead of convergence.
DCT optimization: the two models pursued different dtype strategies, and switching between them lost optimizations each model had already found on its own.

blocks.text: A representative conflict, alternating between incompatible algorithms iteration to iteration:

blocks.html:
# Iteration N: Gemini suggests BFS
queue = deque([start])  # BFS approach

# Iteration N+1: Qwen suggests Union-Find
parent = list(range(n))  # Different algorithm!

# Result: Hybrid mess that optimizes neither

blocks.text: Three failure modes recurred across the ensemble runs:

items: Algorithm conflicts: BFS versus Union-Find approaches proposed for the same task.
Optimization conflicts: memory-oriented edits competing with compute-oriented edits.
Style conflicts: functional versus imperative code patterns alternating across iterations.

blocks.text: The configuration that performed best across the sweep:

blocks.html:
# Optimal configuration discovered
max_iterations: 200  # More is better
diff_based_evolution: true  # For capable models
temperature: 0.4  # For Gemini, 0.6 for others
max_tokens: 16000  # Sweet spot
num_top_programs: 3
num_islands: 4
migration_interval: 20
migration_rate: 0.1
include_artifacts: true  # Critical for performance

items: Four islands evolve in parallel to maintain solution diversity.
Migration every 20 iterations prevents premature convergence to a single strategy.
Each island can discover a different solution independently.
The best program is tracked globally across all islands.
Stage 1: quick syntax and import validation, under 1 second.
Stage 2: small test cases, under 10 seconds.
Stage 3: the full benchmark suite, under 60 seconds.

blocks.text: Failing fast at the earlier, cheaper stages saved roughly 70% of total evaluation time.

items: Iteration count: 200 iterations reached 2.04x versus 1.64x for 100 iterations, a 24% improvement.
Model specialization: Qwen3-Coder, a coding-specialized model, outperformed larger general-purpose models.
Temperature: results varied by setting. The best individual run was at 0.4, though variance was high.
Evolution strategy: diff-based evolution worked better for strong coding models, full rewrite for weaker ones.
Parallelism: serial evaluation degraded performance by 47 to 50% and increased wall-clock time 14x.
Ensemble results: combining models reached 1.23x, below either model's individual score of 1.64x and 1.41x.
Models discovered genuinely different algorithmic approaches to the same task, such as BFS versus Union-Find for graph problems.
Hardware-bound tasks like SHA256 showed minimal improvement across every configuration tested.
Including artifacts in the evaluation feedback improved performance by roughly 17%.
A migration rate of 0.1 outperformed 0.2 across the tested configurations.

blocks.text: This study has two follow-ups in progress. EvolveBench extends the same evaluation to 11 real-world open-source repositories (SymPy, NetworkX, pandas, and others) instead of AlgoTune's synthetic tasks, and compares hand-written evaluators against LLM-generated ones. It also motivated three new capabilities added to OpenEvolve since this study:

items: Adaptive ensembles that pick which model proposes each edit by Thompson sampling, instead of running every model every iteration. This reverses the naive-ensemble underperformance found above on most re-tested tasks.
Novelty detection, which rejects near-duplicate candidates before they consume an evaluation.
Two-phase warmup optimization, which automates the kind of manual hyperparameter sweeps used in Phases 2 and 3 above.

footnotes.text: "Artifacts" in OpenEvolve are debugging outputs (stack traces, intermediate values, timing breakdowns) that a program can return during evaluation, alongside its score. They give the LLM more to reason about than a bare number, which is why removing them cost 17% of AlgoTune score.

The original report includes a horizontal bar chart ranking all 29 experiments by AlgoTune score, colored by performance band (green above 1.5x, blue 1.2 to 1.5x, orange 1.0 to 1.2x, red below 1.0x). It is not reproduced here. The same rankings are covered by the top-performers table and the per-phase results below.
Qwen3-Coder was only evaluated at temperature 0.6, not swept the way Gemini was at 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8. Its 1.41x score may not reflect this model's true optimum.
